summary: Yellow-groove bamboo is a running bamboo that spreads underground and forms dense thickets with little or nothing growing beneath them. Stands larger than a quarter acre are known from Nassau County, New York. New York's official ranking lists it as "Not Assessable", because no one has conclusively shown it spreading into the wild on its own, without people planting or moving it.
history: Yellow-groove bamboo is native to China. Bamboos in this group are among the most popular sold, and they spread mainly when people plant them or move soil containing their underground stems. Floodwaters can sometimes carry pieces downstream.

handling.text: Small patches can be controlled by repeated cutting or mowing, several times each growing season for several years, until the underground stems run out of energy. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
